meaning_en: Poverty and need can make an honest person do wrong.
conversation:
Anjali: Raju used to top his class. Now I see him running errands for the local goons.
Headmaster: His father lost his job at the jute mill and they have nothing to eat. Obhabe shobhab noshto.
correct: Poverty has pushed a good boy like Raju into bad company.
literal: Where things are scarce, nature itself goes to ruin.
plausible: Raju was always a troublemaker and has now shown his true colours.

meaning_en: Wasting something precious on people who can't appreciate it.
conversation:
Dadu: I gave Bapan my collection of old Bengali magazines from the 1950s.
Thakuma: And he sold them to the scrap-paper man for forty rupees. Ulubone mukto chhorano.
correct: Giving rare magazines to Bapan was a waste, because he couldn't value them.
literal: Pearls were thrown away carelessly into a field of tall reeds.
plausible: Bapan made a smart deal by selling off the old magazines.

meaning_en: Adding insult to injury.
conversation:
Bappa: I lost my job on Monday, and on Tuesday the landlord raised the rent by three thousand.
Shibu: What cruel timing. Kata ghaye nuner chhite.
correct: The rent hike makes Bappa's already bad situation even more painful.
literal: Some salt has been sprinkled right over a fresh cut wound.
plausible: The rent hike is fair and really has nothing to do with Bappa's troubles.

meaning_en: Adding insult to injury.
conversation:
Arjun: Our goalkeeper was already crying after the final, and then the coach blamed him on live TV.
Nirmal: Poor fellow. Kata ghaye nuner chhite.
correct: The coach's public blame made the goalkeeper's pain even worse.
literal: Someone has rubbed some salt directly into an open wound.
plausible: The coach's criticism will only make the goalkeeper mentally stronger.

meaning_en: Catch the small one and the big one behind it gets exposed too.
conversation:
Tania: The police only arrested a small-time drug seller near the station.
Ghosh-da: Keep following the story. He'll lead them to the supplier. Kan tanle matha ashe.
correct: The small seller's arrest will lead the police to the big supplier behind him.
literal: Pulling hard on an ear brings the whole head along with it.
plausible: The seller's arrest is a minor event that won't lead anywhere.

meaning_en: Counting your chickens before they hatch.
conversation:
Shubho: Once my band wins the college competition, I'll drop out and go on a tour across India.
Rimjhim: The auditions haven't even started! Gachhe kanthal gonphe tel.
correct: Shubho is making big plans around a win that hasn't happened yet.
literal: Someone oils his moustache while the jackfruit is still on the tree.
plausible: Shubho has a clear and sensible plan for his music career.

meaning_en: Counting your chickens before they hatch.
conversation:
Sharmila: Sanyal-babu has already booked a wedding hall for his daughter and that boy from Durgapur.
Paltu: The girl hasn't even met the boy yet! Gachhe kanthal gonphe tel.
correct: Sanyal-babu is preparing for a wedding that hasn't even been agreed.
literal: A man oils his moustache though the jackfruit is still hanging on the tree.
plausible: Sanyal-babu is a careful father who plans everything well in advance.

meaning_en: Counting your chickens before they hatch.
conversation:
Jhunu: Your father bought one lottery ticket and is already arguing about which car to buy.
Babai: The draw isn't until next month! Gachhe kanthal gonphe tel.
correct: He is planning to spend prize money he hasn't won and probably never will.
literal: Someone has oiled his moustache before the jackfruit has even been picked from the tree.
plausible: He is sensibly deciding well in advance how to use the prize money.

proverb_bn: ঠাকুর ঘরে কে? আমি কলা খাই না
romanised: Thakur ghore ke? Ami kola khai na.
meaning_en: A guilty person gives themselves away by denying something no one accused them of.
conversation:
Rakhi: Someone deleted the shared sales file this morning.
Bikram: Don't look at me! I never even opened that folder today!
Supriya: Nobody asked you, Bikram. Thakur ghore ke? Ami kola khai na.
correct: Bikram's eager denial, before anyone accused him, suggests he deleted the file.
literal: Someone in the prayer room is saying they don't eat bananas.
plausible: Bikram is clearly innocent, because he says he never opened the folder.

meaning_en: Give someone an inch and they take a mile.
conversation:
Jhuma: We let our cousin keep his bike in our garage for a week.
Partha: Now he's moved his car in too, and he wants a spare key to the house. Boshte pele shute chay.
correct: The cousin keeps demanding more after being given a small favour.
literal: Someone who is offered a seat wants to lie down and stretch out instead.
plausible: The cousin is in real trouble and genuinely needs more help.

meaning_en: Giving more to, or flattering, those who already have plenty.
conversation:
Soma: The company gave the biggest bonus to the CEO's nephew, who already earns twice what we do.
Biswajit: And the cleaners didn't even get a box of sweets for Pujo. Tela mathay tel deoa.
correct: The company keeps rewarding someone who already has plenty, while ignoring those in need.
literal: Pouring more oil onto hair that is already well oiled and dripping.
plausible: The CEO's nephew deserved the bonus because he works the hardest of all.

meaning_en: Giving more to, or flattering, those who already have plenty.
conversation:
Bonani: Mejo-mashi gave a gold chain to her rich nephew from Delhi and nothing to the twins from the village.
Tapan: That's how she is. Tela mathay tel deoa.
correct: Mejo-mashi lavishes gifts on the rich relative while ignoring the ones who need them.
literal: More oil is being poured onto a head that is already very oily indeed.
plausible: Mejo-mashi's expensive gift shows that she loves all her nephews equally.

meaning_en: Nurturing someone who will later betray you.
conversation:
Ruma: Tarun-babu trained that boy for ten years and made him his right-hand man.
Ashok: And now the boy has started his own firm and taken all of Tarun-babu's clients with him. Dudhkola diye kalshap posha.
correct: Tarun-babu raised and trusted someone who has now betrayed him.
literal: Someone fed milk and bananas to a deadly snake in order to raise it.
plausible: The young man has fairly earned his success through hard work.

proverb_bn: দুষ্ট গরুর চেয়ে শূন্য গোয়াল ভালো
romanised: Dushto gorur cheye shunyo goal bhalo.
meaning_en: Better to have no one than a troublesome or bad companion.
conversation:
Mohua: The new tenant pays late, fights with the neighbours and has broken two windows. But if he leaves, the flat will be empty.
Kanai: Then let it stay empty for a while. Dushto gorur cheye shunyo goal bhalo.
correct: Having no tenant is better than keeping a troublesome one.
literal: A shed with no cattle is preferable to keeping a vicious cow.
plausible: Any tenant is better than none, so they should keep him.

proverb_bn: নেই মামার চেয়ে কানা মামা ভালো
romanised: Nei mamar cheye kana mama bhalo.
meaning_en: Something is better than nothing.
conversation:
Tanushree: The only flat I found near the office is tiny, on the fifth floor, with no lift.
Ma: Take it for now. It beats travelling three hours every day. Nei mamar cheye kana mama bhalo.
correct: An imperfect flat is better than having no flat near the office at all.
literal: It is better to have a half-blind maternal uncle than to have no uncle at all.
plausible: Tanushree should keep searching until she finds the perfect flat.

proverb_bn: নেই মামার চেয়ে কানা মামা ভালো
romanised: Nei mamar cheye kana mama bhalo.
meaning_en: Something is better than nothing.
conversation:
Ritu: Pinku-da is giving me his old laptop. It's slow and the battery barely lasts.
Baba: You've been doing your assignments on your phone till now. Nei mamar cheye kana mama bhalo.
correct: A slow old laptop is still better for Ritu than having none.
literal: An uncle with one bad eye is better than not having an uncle at all.
plausible: Ritu should refuse the laptop and wait for a new one.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Anjali: Boro-pishi told everyone at the wedding that our new bou is unlucky because it rained.
Ritwik: Boro-pishi says something like that at every wedding. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Ritwik thinks Boro-pishi's remark is silly talk that nobody should take to heart.
literal: There is nothing at all that a madman won't say, and nothing that a goat won't chew.
plausible: Ritwik agrees that the rain on the wedding day really was a bad sign.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Rafiq: The man in the next flat is telling the whole building that I'm a spy because I work at night.
Nadia: He also says his cat talks to him. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Nadia tells Rafiq not to worry about the neighbour's absurd accusation.
literal: Crazy people say anything at all, just as goats eat anything.
plausible: Nadia thinks Rafiq should stop working at night so as to avoid suspicion.

meaning_en: A precious thing in the hands of someone who can't value it.
conversation:
Priya: Management gave the new analytics software licence to Sen-babu, who still prints out every email.
Arindam: And it hasn't even been opened on his laptop. Banorer golay muktor mala.
correct: Expensive software has gone to someone who can't make any use of it.
literal: Pearls have been hung around the neck of a little monkey.
plausible: Sen-babu is secretly the best person in the office to use the software.

meaning_en: A precious thing in the hands of someone who can't value it.
conversation:
Kaushik: My cousin inherited our grandfather's old sitar.
Rupa: The same cousin who hangs his wet towels on it to dry? Banorer golay muktor mala.
correct: The cousin doesn't value the precious sitar he inherited.
literal: A monkey has been given a string of pearls to wear.
plausible: The cousin is planning to become a professional sitar player.

meaning_en: Beggars can't be choosers.
conversation:
Selina: The volunteers painted the school walls for free, but the colour is a bit dull.
Habib: We didn't have any budget at all. Bhikkhar chal kanra ar akanra.
correct: Habib says they can't be choosy about work done for free.
literal: Rice given to a beggar can be either husked or still in its husk.
plausible: Habib wants the volunteers to repaint the walls in a brighter colour.

meaning_en: Meddling in matters far above one's own concern.
conversation:
Kartik: Nemai-da at the tea stall argues all day about what the American central bank should do.
Bishu: He still hasn't paid back the five hundred rupees he owes me. Adar byaparir jahajer khobor.
correct: Nemai-da busies himself with huge matters that have nothing to do with him.
literal: A man who trades in ginger keeps asking for news of the ships.
plausible: Nemai-da is an expert whose views on banking are worth hearing.

meaning_en: Talent or character shows early on.
conversation:
Gopa: The new tenant's son is only six and he already picks fights with every child in the lane.
Chandana: Uthti mulo pottonei chena jay. Wait till he's sixteen.
correct: The boy's behaviour already hints at the kind of person he will become.
literal: You can tell how a radish will turn out just from its very first sprouts.
plausible: Chandana thinks the boy will calm down as he grows older.

meaning_en: A quarrel or problem always involves both sides.
conversation:
Soma: Mrs Dutta says the Boses started the fight over the parking spot.
Pradip: And the Boses say the Duttas started it. Ek hate tali baje na.
correct: Pradip thinks both families share the blame for the fight.
literal: You can't make a clapping sound with just one hand on its own.
plausible: Pradip believes the Boses alone are to blame for it.

meaning_en: A quarrel or problem always involves both sides.
conversation:
Mitu: Ma, Arko never listens. Every argument we have is his fault.
Ma: And you hang up on him every single time. Ek hate tali baje na.
correct: Ma thinks Mitu also plays a part in the arguments.
literal: One palm on its own cannot produce the sound of a clap.
plausible: Ma agrees that Arko is entirely at fault here.

meaning_en: A quarrel or problem always involves both sides.
conversation:
Ruma: They've arrested the officer who took the bribe.
Faisal: And what about the company that paid it? Ek hate tali baje na.
correct: Faisal thinks the company that paid the bribe is just as guilty.
literal: To make a clapping sound you really need more than just one hand.
plausible: Faisal is satisfied that justice has now been done.

proverb_bn: একা রামে রক্ষা নেই, সুগ্রীব দোসর
romanised: Eka Rame rokkha nei, Sugriv doshor.
meaning_en: One troublemaker was already too much, and now a second one has joined.
conversation:
Sreya: Biswas-babu rejects every design we make anyway. Now head office is sending a second reviewer.
Tanmoy: And I hear he's even stricter. Eka Rame rokkha nei, Sugriv doshor.
correct: One difficult reviewer was hard enough, and now another tough one is joining.
literal: There was no escape from Ram already, and now Sugriva has become his companion.
plausible: The second reviewer will make it easier to get designs approved.

meaning_en: People don't value the talent of someone they know well; no prophet is honoured at home.
conversation:
Moni: Our neighbour's daughter sings at concerts in Mumbai, but nobody at the local puja ever asks her to sing.
Bappaditya: Genyo jogi bhikh pay na.
correct: Her own neighbourhood doesn't appreciate the talent others admire.
literal: A yogi from the village gets no offerings from anyone.
plausible: The puja committee thinks that she sings rather badly.

meaning_en: Getting involved with a lowly person only dirties your own name.
conversation:
Sharmin: The candidate who spreads fake news has challenged you to a TV debate.
Rezaul: Debating him only gives him what he wants. Chhuncho mere hat gondho.
correct: Rezaul feels engaging with the dishonest candidate would only tarnish his name.
literal: Your hand smells unpleasant for a long time after you kill a muskrat.
plausible: Rezaul is worried that he is simply not prepared enough for a TV debate.

proverb_bn: দাঁত থাকতে দাঁতের মর্যাদা বোঝে না
romanised: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
meaning_en: We don't value what we have until we lose it.
conversation:
Soumi: Your knee hurts so much that you can't even climb the stairs now?
Riju: For years the doctor told me to lose weight, and I ignored him. Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
correct: Riju didn't look after his knees while they were healthy, and only understands now.
literal: People don't respect their own teeth while the teeth are still firmly in their mouths.
plausible: Riju thinks the doctor gave him the wrong advice about losing weight.

proverb_bn: দাঁত থাকতে দাঁতের মর্যাদা বোঝে না
romanised: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
meaning_en: We don't value what we have until we lose it.
conversation:
Arif: I left my old job because the manager was strict, but at least he trained us properly. My new boss doesn't care at all.
Moushumi: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
correct: Arif didn't appreciate his old manager until he no longer had him.
literal: Teeth are not valued while they are still there in the mouth.
plausible: Moushumi thinks Arif's new boss will turn out to be better in the end.

meaning_en: Settling for a poor substitute for what you really wanted.
conversation:
Ritika: You couldn't get tickets for the Arijit concert, so you're watching his old videos on YouTube all night?
Sayantan: What else can I do? Dudher shadh ghole metano.
correct: Sayantan is settling for a poor substitute for the concert he wanted.
literal: Someone who wanted milk satisfies the craving with a glass of buttermilk.
plausible: Sayantan actually prefers watching videos to live concerts.

meaning_en: Sudden arrogance or overreaching comes just before a downfall.
conversation:
Alo: Since Bablu won the local election, he's been insulting everyone and even threatening the old councillor.
Sukhen: Pipilikar pakha othe moribar tore. Let's see how long he lasts.
correct: Bablu's sudden arrogance is a sign that his downfall is coming.
literal: An ant grows its wings only when it is about to die.
plausible: Sukhen thinks Bablu will remain a powerful leader for many years.

meaning_en: Sudden arrogance or overreaching comes just before a downfall.
conversation:
Liton: That local goon Kalu has started extorting money even from the police constables now.
Shaon: Pipilikar pakha othe moribar tore. His days are numbered.
correct: Kalu's growing arrogance signals that his end is near.
literal: The wings of an ant come out so that it can die.
plausible: Shaon thinks Kalu has become too powerful to be stopped.

proverb_bn: ভাত ছড়ালে কাকের অভাব হয় না
romanised: Bhat chhorale kaker obhab hoy na.
meaning_en: Where there is money or favours, hangers-on are never lacking.
conversation:
Sutapa: Since Bhola won the lottery, people he hasn't seen in years keep turning up at his door.
Mridul: Bhat chhorale kaker obhab hoy na.
correct: Now that Bhola has money, opportunistic hangers-on are flocking to him.
literal: If you scatter rice, there are always plenty of crows.
plausible: Mridul thinks Bhola's old friends have genuinely missed him.

proverb_bn: ভাত ছড়ালে কাকের অভাব হয় না
romanised: Bhat chhorale kaker obhab hoy na.
meaning_en: Where there is money or favours, hangers-on are never lacking.
conversation:
Mousumi: Ever since he got the contracts, the minister's nephew has twenty 'advisers' following him everywhere.
Tamal: Bhat chhorale kaker obhab hoy na.
correct: His access to contracts attracts people who want a share of the benefits.
literal: Crows are never in short supply wherever rice has been spread.
plausible: The nephew needs twenty advisers because his new work is very complex indeed.

meaning_en: Words alone, without real action or payment, get nothing done.
conversation:
Mala: The contractor keeps promising to finish the bathroom next week, but nothing happens.
Sushanta: Hold back his payment until he does. Shukno kothay chinre bheje na.
correct: Promises alone will not get the bathroom finished; real action is needed.
literal: Flattened rice does not get soaked by talking dry words at it.
plausible: Sushanta trusts that the contractor will finish next week.

proverb_bn: যেখানে বাঘের ভয়, সেখানে সন্ধ্যা হয়
romanised: Jekhane bagher bhoy, shekhane shondhya hoy.
meaning_en: Trouble strikes exactly where and when you fear it most.
conversation:
Lipi: How did the presentation go?
Sajal: The one slide I wasn't sure about is exactly the one the director asked about. Jekhane bagher bhoy, shekhane shondhya hoy.
correct: The director questioned Sajal on exactly the part he feared most.
literal: Evening falls just where the tiger is most feared.
plausible: Sajal was fully prepared for the director's question.

meaning_en: Only a worthy person recognises worth in another.
conversation:
Arnab: Nobody noticed Rana's songs on social media, but Ustad Rashid heard one and took him on as a student.
Sharmistha: Rotone roton chene.
correct: It took a truly great musician to recognise Rana's talent.
literal: One jewel can tell another jewel apart from the rest.
plausible: Ustad Rashid took Rana only because no other student applied.

proverb_bn: সাপ হয়ে কাটে, ওঝা হয়ে ঝাড়ে
romanised: Shap hoye kate, ojha hoye jhare.
meaning_en: Creating a problem and then posing as the one who solves it.
conversation:
Chhanda: Paltu-da spread that rumour about my son, and now he's going around telling everyone he'll clear our name.
Mohit: Shap hoye kate, ojha hoye jhare.
correct: Paltu-da created the trouble himself and now pretends to be the rescuer.
literal: A snake bites someone and then cures the bite as an exorcist.
plausible: Mohit thinks Paltu-da is truly trying to help their family.

meaning_en: Rejecting good fortune that has come to you.
conversation:
Shilpi: A big hotel offered to buy all our sweets every month, and Kaka refused because he doesn't like the manager.
Raju: Hater Lokkhi paye thela.
correct: Kaka is rejecting a lucky business opportunity over a small dislike.
literal: The goddess Lakshmi, held in one's hand, is pushed away with the foot.
plausible: Raju thinks the hotel's offer was really some kind of trap.

meaning_en: Trying for more and losing everything.
conversation:
Babai: I quit my job for the new offer, but the new company withdrew it before I could join.
Rinki: So amo gelo chhalao gelo.
correct: Babai has ended up with neither the old job nor the new one.
literal: He lost the mango and the jute bag along with it.
plausible: Babai can easily go back to his old job if he wants.

proverb_bn: কাজের বেলায় কাজি, কাজ ফুরোলে পাজি
romanised: Kajer belay kaji, kaj phurole paji.
meaning_en: People value you only while they need you.
conversation:
Sumaiya: Rafi borrowed my notes before every exam, and now that exams are over he ignores me in the corridor.
Nayeem: Kajer belay kaji, kaj phurole paji.
correct: Rafi was friendly only while he needed Sumaiya's notes.
literal: Someone is a qazi at work time and a villain when the work is done.
plausible: Nayeem thinks Rafi is just shy now that the exams are over.

meaning_en: One trouble piled on top of another.
conversation:
Reshma: The project was already behind schedule, and now our lead developer has resigned.
Kunal: Goder upor bishphonra.
correct: The resignation makes an already bad situation even worse.
literal: A poisonous boil sits on a leg swollen with elephantiasis.
plausible: Kunal thinks the resignation will help the project finish faster.

meaning_en: One trouble piled on top of another.
conversation:
Farzana: The rain flooded our shop, and now the landlord wants to raise the rent.
Aminul: Goder upor bishphonra.
correct: One trouble has been heaped on another for their shop.
literal: There is a painful boil right on top of a swelling.
plausible: Aminul thinks the rent rise is fair after the landlord's repairs.

meaning_en: Becoming lazy or helpless as soon as help is available.
conversation:
Selina: Abba carried his own bags everywhere, but now that my brother is visiting he can't even lift a glass of water.
Nazrul: Ghora dekhle khonra.
correct: Abba is acting helpless because help has arrived.
literal: A person goes lame at the mere sight of a horse nearby.
plausible: Abba has suddenly fallen seriously ill this week.

meaning_en: A person who is well known needs no proof of identity or credentials.
conversation:
Rahul: Did Mitali Sen, who has sung in a hundred films, really have to audition for this one?
Pallabi: Of course not. Chena bamuner poite lage na.
correct: A singer as established as she is doesn't need to prove her ability.
literal: A familiar Brahmin can go about his day without wearing his sacred thread.
plausible: Pallabi thinks every singer must audition, however famous.

meaning_en: Someone who is used only for the lowliest, thankless jobs.
conversation:
Anwara: The party only calls Jalal-bhai when they need someone to put up posters at midnight.
Rafiqul: Chhai phelte bhanga kulo. He never gets a ticket to contest the election.
correct: Jalal-bhai is used by the party only for thankless grunt work.
literal: A cracked winnowing fan serves to throw away ashes.
plausible: Rafiqul thinks the party is grooming Jalal-bhai for a top post.

proverb_bn: যারে দেখতে নারি, তার চলন বাঁকা
romanised: Jare dekhte nari, tar cholon banka.
meaning_en: Everything a disliked person does looks wrong.
conversation:
Mukta: If our new neighbours plant flowers, Mrs Rahman says they're showing off; if they keep quiet, she calls them rude.
Habib: Jare dekhte nari, tar cholon banka.
correct: Mrs Rahman dislikes the new neighbours, so she finds fault in everything they do.
literal: The one I can't bear to look at walks crookedly down the road.
plausible: Habib thinks the new neighbours really are rude and showing off.

meaning_en: Going off on an irrelevant tangent.
conversation:
Farhana: The viva was on my thesis, and the external examiner kept asking about my school days in Sylhet.
Rakib: Examiners do that sometimes. Dhan bhante Shiber git.
correct: The examiner wandered into topics unrelated to the thesis.
literal: The examiner was singing a song to Shiva while he husked the rice paddy.
plausible: Rakib thinks the school questions were part of the formal viva.

meaning_en: Getting something trivial in return for a great loss.
conversation:
Rohit: Mohun Bagan sold their best striker and got a second-division defender in return.
Asif: Naker bodole norun. The fans are furious.
correct: The club gave up its most valuable player for something nearly worthless.
literal: The club handed over its nose and got a nail-cutter back.
plausible: Asif thinks the defender will strengthen the team considerably.

meaning_en: People put up with harsh treatment from those who provide for them.
conversation:
Rafiq: Your mother-in-law scolds you all day, yet you never say a word back.
Shirin: She also feeds my children and pays their school fees. Pete khele pithe shoy.
correct: Shirin bears the scolding because her mother-in-law provides for them.
literal: Shirin's back endures the blows because her belly is fed.
plausible: Shirin secretly plans to move out of her mother-in-law's house very soon.

meaning_en: Good news that doesn't benefit someone means nothing to them.
conversation:
Aritra: The girls' hostel is getting new air conditioners next month.
Junaid: And we live in the boys' block. Bel pakle kaker ki?
correct: The new air conditioners won't help Junaid, so they don't matter to him.
literal: A crow sitting nearby gains nothing when the wood apple on the tree ripens.
plausible: Junaid is pleased that the hostel is getting air conditioning.

meaning_en: Too proud or stubborn to admit defeat or a mistake.
conversation:
Mithun: Your sister clearly regrets quitting her job, but she keeps telling everyone it was the best decision.
Shabnam: Bhangbe tobu mochkabe na. That's my sister.
correct: Shabnam's sister is too proud to admit she made a mistake.
literal: Shabnam's sister would break apart before she would bend.
plausible: Shabnam thinks her sister genuinely has no regrets about quitting her job.

meaning_en: Something once great keeps its value even after its decline.
conversation:
Sourav: The old zamindar house in Shobhabazar is falling apart, yet a film company paid huge money to shoot there.
Ananya: Of course. Mora hati lakh taka.
correct: Even in decline, the grand old house is still very valuable.
literal: Even a dead elephant can be sold for a lakh of rupees in the market.
plausible: Ananya thinks the film company has wasted its money on the house.

meaning_en: Something once great keeps its value even after its decline.
conversation:
Sayan: That actor hasn't had a hit in fifteen years, and he still got paid more than the new hero.
Rehana: Mora hati lakh taka.
correct: Though past his prime, the once-great actor still commands a high price.
literal: Even when an elephant dies, it still fetches a lakh of rupees.
plausible: Rehana thinks the producers are paying the actor out of pity.

meaning_en: Using far too much force for a small problem.

Rituparna: Mosha marte kaman daga.

proverb_bn: যার বিয়ে তার হুঁশ নেই, পাড়াপড়শির ঘুম নেই

proverb_bn: রাজায় রাজায় যুদ্ধ হয়, উলুখাগড়ার প্রাণ যায়

proverb_bn: রাজায় রাজায় যুদ্ধ হয়, উলুখাগড়ার প্রাণ যায়

meaning_en: People will pay any price for something they love.

meaning_en: Repeated copying or retelling distorts the original.

proverb_bn: কানে দিয়েছি তুলো, পিঠে বেঁধেছি কুলো

meaning_en: Someone acts bold only because of a powerful backer.

meaning_en: Encouraging someone into a risky position and then abandoning them.

meaning_en: Encouraging someone into a risky position and then abandoning them.

meaning_en: Everyone is guilty; if you remove the dishonest, no one is left.

meaning_en: We put up with the faults of those who are useful to us.

plausible: Ankana thinks the boss hasn't noticed the salesman's insults.

plausible: Hasina thinks the business is a much better choice for the son.

meaning_en: Ruining something just when it is about to bear fruit.

proverb_bn: ভাত দেওয়ার ভাতার নয়, কিল মারার গোঁসাই

proverb_bn: যে যায় লঙ্কায় সেই হয় রাবণ

proverb_bn: একে মা মনসা, তায় ধুনোর গন্ধ

proverb_bn: একে মা মনসা, তায় ধুনোর গন্ধ

plausible: Rumana thinks the embassy will reopen and call him soon.

proverb_bn: কপালে নেই ঘি, ঠকঠকালে হবে কী

plausible: Rahela thinks the son will start listening once he marries.

meaning_en: A self-appointed leader whom no one recognises.

meaning_en: An outstanding person from humble or unlikely surroundings.

meaning_en: An outstanding person from humble or unlikely surroundings.

meaning_en: You see the easy gain but not the danger that comes with it.

meaning_en: You see the easy gain but not the danger that comes with it.

meaning_en: Criticising one person so that another gets the message.
conversation:
Aparna: The coach shouted at the juniors for skipping practice, while the captain, who skips the most, sat right there.
Rumman: Jhike mere bouke shekhano.
correct: The coach scolded the juniors so the captain would get the message.
literal: The coach was beating the maid to teach a lesson to the daughter-in-law.
plausible: Rumman thinks the coach is afraid to scold the captain.

proverb_bn: ঢাল নেই তলোয়ার নেই নিধিরাম সর্দার
romanised: Dhal nei tolowar nei Nidhiram shordar.
meaning_en: A grand title with no real means or power.
conversation:
Mizanur: My cousin was made chairman of the village flood committee, but there's no boat, no money and no volunteers.
Kulsum: Dhal nei tolowar nei Nidhiram shordar.
correct: The cousin holds a fine title but has no means to do anything.
literal: The cousin is like a commander with no shield and no sword to fight with.
plausible: Kulsum thinks the cousin will manage the floods very well.

proverb_bn: ঢাল নেই তলোয়ার নেই নিধিরাম সর্দার
romanised: Dhal nei tolowar nei Nidhiram shordar.
meaning_en: A grand title with no real means or power.
conversation:
Rishav: The new 'Minister of Sports' in our student union has no funds, no ground and no say in anything.
Nadira: Dhal nei tolowar nei Nidhiram shordar.
correct: He has an impressive title but no real power or means at all.
literal: He is a commander without either a shield or a sword.
plausible: Nadira thinks the sports minister will soon organise a big tournament.

meaning_en: Wasting effort or resources on something useless.
conversation:
Jamil: The ministry keeps funding that factory, though it hasn't produced anything for ten years.
Sufia: Bhoshme ghi dhala.
correct: The ministry is wasting money on something completely useless.
literal: The ministry keeps pouring precious ghee onto a pile of dead ashes.
plausible: Sufia thinks the factory will start producing again soon.

meaning_en: Only the sufferer truly knows the suffering.
conversation:
Saikat: Everyone tells Ma to 'just relax' about Dada's illness. They don't sit with him at the hospital every night.
Urmila: Jar jala shei bojhe.
correct: Only Ma, who is going through it, truly knows how painful it is.
literal: Only a person whose skin has actually been burned knows how much it hurts.
plausible: Urmila agrees that Ma really should try to relax a lot more.

meaning_en: Only the sufferer truly knows the suffering.
conversation:
Rezaul: My neighbours say the river erosion isn't that bad. Their houses are on the high road; ours fell into the river.
Banu: Jar jala shei bojhe.
correct: Only those who suffer the loss truly know how painful it is.
literal: Only the one who has been burnt knows how a burn feels.
plausible: Banu thinks the neighbours are right that the erosion is not so bad.

meaning_en: An extremely meek person who never protests.
conversation:
Shafayet: The supervisor takes credit for all of Habib's work, and Habib just smiles and keeps working.
Rokshana: Sat chore ra nei.
correct: Habib is so meek that he never protests about anything.
literal: Even after being slapped seven times, Habib doesn't make a single sound.
plausible: Rokshana thinks Habib is happy to share credit with the supervisor.

meaning_en: Using one harmful thing to get rid of another.
conversation:
Sujoy: The builder's goons were harassing us, so my uncle called the local dada to scare them off.
Aditi: Kanta diye kanta tola.
correct: The uncle used one troublemaker to get rid of another.
literal: The uncle used one sharp thorn to pull out another thorn.
plausible: Aditi thinks the local dada is a kind man who helps the neighbourhood.

meaning_en: Using one harmful thing to get rid of another.
conversation:
Pratyush: My doctor gave me one medicine for the acidity caused by my painkillers, and now that one makes me dizzy.
Tahmid: Kanta diye kanta tola.
correct: One harmful medicine is being used to fix the harm of another.
literal: The doctor pulled out one thorn by digging in with another sharp thorn.
plausible: Tahmid thinks the dizziness has nothing to do with the medicine.

meaning_en: Trying to force a dull person to become brilliant.
conversation:
Swarnali: Mrs Sen has hired four tutors to make her son crack IIT, and he can't even do class-eight maths.
Hirak: Gadha pitiye ghora kora.
correct: She is trying to force a weak student to become brilliant.
literal: Mrs Sen is beating a donkey hard in the hope of turning it into a horse.
plausible: Hirak thinks four tutors will surely get the boy into IIT.

meaning_en: Trying to force a dull person to become brilliant.
conversation:
Monir: The club's owner keeps paying coaches to turn his nephew into a striker, but the boy can't even kick straight.
Nazneen: Gadha pitiye ghora kora.
correct: The owner is trying to force a talentless boy into a star.
literal: The owner keeps beating a donkey to make it into a horse.
plausible: Nazneen thinks the nephew is just one good coach away from greatness.

meaning_en: Trying to force a dull person to become brilliant.
conversation:
Anurag: The company sent the new hire to five leadership trainings, but he still can't run a ten-minute meeting.
Samiha: Gadha pitiye ghora kora.
correct: The company is trying to force an unsuitable person into a leader.
literal: They are beating a donkey in the hope it turns into a horse.
plausible: Samiha thinks one more training will make him a great leader.

meaning_en: Nobody is perfect.
conversation:
Joydeb: Our perfect topper Ritwika failed her driving test three times!
Srabani: Chandero kolongko achhe.
correct: Even someone as brilliant as Ritwika has her own flaws.
literal: Even the bright full moon has a dark stain on its face.
plausible: Srabani thinks Ritwika failed on purpose so she wouldn't have to drive.

meaning_en: Nobody is perfect.
conversation:
Rajashree: That famous actor everyone calls a saint was caught skipping his taxes.
Ibrahim: Chandero kolongko achhe.
correct: Even an actor admired as a saint turns out to have his flaws.
literal: If you look closely, even the bright moon has a dark stain on its surface.
plausible: Ibrahim thinks the tax story about the actor is fake news.

meaning_en: A subordinate who is more arrogant than the boss.
conversation:
Supratim: The minister himself was polite to us, but his PA made us wait three hours and shouted at the guard.
Mallika: Basher cheye konchi dor.
correct: The minister's PA is more arrogant than the minister himself.
literal: The thin twig has turned out to be even tougher than the bamboo it grew from.
plausible: Mallika thinks the PA was only protecting the busy minister.

meaning_en: A subordinate who is more arrogant than the boss.
conversation:
Sohrab: The chairman listens to everyone, but his nephew who runs the office talks to people like they're servants.
Taslima: Basher cheye konchi dor.
correct: The nephew is far more arrogant than the chairman he works for.
literal: The twig is stronger and tougher than the bamboo itself.
plausible: Taslima thinks the nephew is strict only because the office is very busy.

meaning_en: A subordinate who is more arrogant than the boss.
conversation:
Arijit: The head chef is friendly, but his assistant yells at every waiter as if he owns the restaurant.
Sharmeen: Basher cheye konchi dor.
correct: The assistant is more arrogant than the head chef he works under.
literal: The little twig is tougher than the bamboo it came from.
plausible: Sharmeen thinks the assistant secretly owns the restaurant.

meaning_en: Those who are patient prevail in the end.
conversation:
Abul: Everyone said the small bookshop would close when the big mall opened. Twenty years later, the mall has shut and the bookshop is still there.
Nilima: Je shoy she roy.
correct: The patient little bookshop outlasted its powerful rival.
literal: Whoever puts up with things is the one who stays on in the same spot.
plausible: Nilima thinks the bookshop survived only because of cheap rent.

meaning_en: Solving a problem without any loss to yourself.
conversation:
Saheb: Ma got the noisy tenant to leave by finding him a cheaper flat nearby. No fight, no lawyer.
Manashi: Shapo more lathio na bhange.
correct: Ma solved the problem without any loss or trouble to herself.
literal: The snake was killed and the stick used to hit it did not break at all.
plausible: Manashi thinks Ma should have taken the tenant to court.

meaning_en: Solving a problem without any loss to yourself.
conversation:
Mahbub: The chairman settled the land dispute by giving each brother a share of the government plot. Both are happy, and he lost nothing.
Pakhi: Shapo more lathio na bhange.
correct: The chairman resolved the dispute without losing anything himself.
literal: The snake is dead, and the stick has not been broken.
plausible: Pakhi thinks the chairman gave away too much of the government plot.

meaning_en: Solving a problem without any loss to yourself.
conversation:
Rajarshi: Our manager got the lazy colleague transferred by recommending him for a 'promotion' in another city.
Mubin: Shapo more lathio na bhange.
correct: The manager got rid of the problem without any cost or trouble to himself.
literal: The snake was killed without the wooden stick ever breaking.
plausible: Mubin thinks the lazy colleague really deserved a promotion.

proverb_bn: বামুন গেল ঘর, তো লাঙল তুলে ধর
romanised: Bamun gelo ghor, to langol tule dhor.
meaning_en: Slacking off as soon as the supervisor leaves.
conversation:
Debarghya: The moment the site supervisor left for lunch, the painters put down their brushes and started playing cards.
Jhumpa: Bamun gelo ghor, to langol tule dhor.
correct: The painters stopped working as soon as their supervisor left.
literal: The Brahmin has gone home, so the plough can be put away.
plausible: Jhumpa thinks the painters had already finished the day's work by lunch.

proverb_bn: বামুন গেল ঘর, তো লাঙল তুলে ধর
romanised: Bamun gelo ghor, to langol tule dhor.
meaning_en: Slacking off as soon as the supervisor leaves.
conversation:
Jewel: As soon as the madam left the classroom, the whole class put their books away and started chatting.
Shapla: Bamun gelo ghor, to langol tule dhor.
correct: The students slacked off the moment their teacher was out of sight.
literal: With the Brahmin gone home, the plough has been set aside.
plausible: Shapla thinks the class had finished its lesson early.

proverb_bn: বামুন গেল ঘর, তো লাঙল তুলে ধর
romanised: Bamun gelo ghor, to langol tule dhor.
meaning_en: Slacking off as soon as the supervisor leaves.
conversation:
Sanchari: The minute our manager's flight took off, half the team logged off and went to the mall.
Adib: Bamun gelo ghor, to langol tule dhor.
correct: The team started slacking off as soon as their manager was gone.
literal: The Brahmin has gone back home, so the plough can now be put down and left.
plausible: Adib thinks the team had been officially given the afternoon off.

meaning_en: The favour of powerful people doesn't last.
conversation:
Sudeep: The MLA used to call Pintu-da his right hand. After the election, he won't even take his calls.
Shrabanti: Boror piriti balir bandh.
correct: The favour of powerful people like the MLA never lasts for long.
literal: The affection of the great is like a dam built out of sand.
plausible: Shrabanti thinks the MLA is simply too busy to answer.

meaning_en: The favour of powerful people doesn't last.
conversation:
Ritabrata: The film star invited our band to every party last year. This year he's found a new band and blocked us.
Sabiha: Boror piriti balir bandh.
correct: The film star's favour faded fast, as such favours always do.
literal: The love of great people is just like a dam built of sand.
plausible: Sabiha thinks the film star blocked the band by mistake and will undo it.

proverb_bn: যার নুন খাই তার গুণ গাই
romanised: Jar nun khai tar gun gai.
meaning_en: Being loyal to the one who provides for you.
conversation:
Sharbari: Everyone complains about the company, but old Haren-babu defends the owner in every meeting.
Debu: He's worked there forty years. Jar nun khai tar gun gai.
correct: Haren-babu stays loyal to the employer who has provided for him.
literal: Haren-babu sings songs in praise of the man whose salt he eats every day.
plausible: Debu thinks Haren-babu is secretly hoping for a promotion soon.

proverb_bn: যার নুন খাই তার গুণ গাই
romanised: Jar nun khai tar gun gai.
meaning_en: Being loyal to the one who provides for you.
conversation:
Mostak: The driver refused to say a word against the minister, even after the minister's scandal came out.
Jahanara: Jar nun khai tar gun gai.
correct: The driver stays loyal to the man who has always provided for him.
literal: The driver sings the praises of the one whose salt he eats.
plausible: Jahanara thinks the driver is too scared of the minister's men to speak.

proverb_bn: যার নুন খাই তার গুণ গাই
romanised: Jar nun khai tar gun gai.
meaning_en: Being loyal to the one who provides for you.
conversation:
Siddhartha: Our cook won't let anyone criticise Didima's recipes. She has lived with us for thirty years.
Mithila: Jar nun khai tar gun gai.
correct: The cook remains loyal to the family that has provided for her for years.
literal: The cook sings the praises of whoever's salt she happens to eat.
plausible: Mithila thinks Didima's recipes really are the best in town.

meaning_en: Sometimes you have to be firm or crooked to get things done.
conversation:
Ripon: The office clerk has been sitting on my file for three months, no matter how nicely I ask.
Selina: Shoja angule ghi othe na.
correct: Asking nicely won't get the file moving; Ripon will have to be firm.
literal: A straight finger cannot scoop the ghee out of the jar.
plausible: Selina thinks the clerk is honestly overloaded with work.

meaning_en: Doing every kind of job, from the most menial to the most sacred.
conversation:
Prithwish: The startup's founder writes the code, mops the floor, pitches to investors and answers customer calls at night.
Liza: Juto shelai theke Chondipath.
correct: The founder does every job there is, from the lowliest to the grandest.
literal: The founder stitches shoes and recites the holy Chandi too.
plausible: Liza thinks the founder should hire more staff before the startup collapses.

meaning_en: An unworthy person can't handle good fortune.
conversation:
Rupankar: Bablu won the lottery in March, and by July he'd crashed two cars and lost everything at the races.
Swastika: Kukurer pete ghi shoy na.
correct: Bablu wasn't fit to handle the sudden good fortune he got.
literal: Rich food like ghee simply never agrees with the stomach of a dog.
plausible: Swastika thinks Bablu was just unlucky at the races.

meaning_en: An unworthy person can't handle good fortune.
conversation:
Mintu: My cousin got a big government post, and within a year he was arrested for taking bribes.
Bilkis: Kukurer pete ghi shoy na.
correct: The cousin wasn't worthy of the good fortune that came to him.
literal: Ghee is far too rich a food for a dog's belly to handle.
plausible: Bilkis thinks the cousin was framed by jealous officers in his department.

meaning_en: An unworthy person can't handle good fortune.
conversation:
Sanjukta: The intern was made team lead after one good project, and now he insults everyone and misses every deadline.
Zarif: Kukurer pete ghi shoy na.
correct: The intern couldn't handle the good fortune he wasn't ready for.
literal: A dog's stomach can't take a rich food like ghee.
plausible: Zarif thinks the intern is simply stressed by the new role.

meaning_en: Greedily wanting it both ways.
conversation:
Tamoghna: My flatmate won't pay for groceries because she 'eats out', but she finishes everything in the fridge.
Sara: Gachhero khabo, tolaro kurobo.
correct: The flatmate wants the benefits without paying her share.
literal: She wants to eat from the tree and gather the fallen fruit as well.
plausible: Sara thinks the flatmate honestly forgets to pay her share.

proverb_bn: হাতি কাদায় পড়লে চামচিকেও লাথি মারে
romanised: Hati kaday porle chamchikeo lathi mare.
meaning_en: When the mighty fall, even the lowly insult them.
conversation:
Zahirul: The big businessman went bankrupt, and now even the tea-stall boy calls him a cheat to his face.
Momtaz: Hati kaday porle chamchikeo lathi mare.
correct: When the mighty fall, even the lowliest people insult them.
literal: Once the elephant has fallen into the mud, even a bat comes along to kick it.
plausible: Momtaz thinks the tea-stall boy was cheated by the businessman.

meaning_en: Making a terrible situation even worse.
conversation:
Supriya: First Baba lost his job, and now the bank has called in the home loan.
Nirmalya: Morar upor khanrar gha.
correct: A bad situation has been made even worse for the family.
literal: Someone struck a heavy sword blow on a person who was already dead.
plausible: Nirmalya thinks the bank is right to call in the loan now.

meaning_en: Making a terrible situation even worse.
conversation:
Oishi: My laptop crashed the night before my thesis deadline, and then the power went out in the whole area.
Fahim: Morar upor khanrar gha.
correct: An already terrible situation became even worse with the power cut.
literal: A heavy sword blow fell on someone who was already dead.
plausible: Fahim thinks Oishi can easily ask for a deadline extension.

meaning_en: Self-reliance is the best help.
conversation:
Selim: No company would hire my sister, so she started selling homemade pickles online, and now she earns more than I do.
Mahfuza: Apon hat Jogonnath.
correct: Selim's sister succeeded by relying on herself instead of others.
literal: The sister's own hand is the god Jagannath himself.
plausible: Mahfuza thinks the pickle business is just a temporary hobby.

meaning_en: Small costs and losses eat up all the gain.
conversation:
Debapriya: Our YouTube channel earned five hundred dollars, but editing software, the mic and the ads cost us four hundred and eighty.
Tasnuva: Labher gur pinpreye khay.
correct: The small expenses have eaten away nearly all of the channel's gain.
literal: Ants have eaten the jaggery that was meant to be the profit.
plausible: Tasnuva thinks they should spend even more on ads next month to grow.

meaning_en: An outsider showing more concern than the person closest to the matter, often fake.
conversation:
Abhik: My neighbour lectures me every day about how to raise my son, as if he's her own child.
Rimpa: Mayer cheye mashir dorod beshi.
correct: An outsider is acting more concerned about the boy than his own parent.
literal: The boy's aunt cares about him more than his own mother does.
plausible: Rimpa thinks the neighbour is giving Abhik genuinely useful parenting advice.

meaning_en: People return to, and blend in with, their own kind.
conversation:
Lutfor: My nephew tried to fit in with the rich kids at university, but by second year he was back with the boys from his hometown.
Joba: Jhanker koi jhanke meshe.
correct: The nephew has gone back to people of his own kind again.
literal: The koi fish that strayed away has swum back to rejoin its own shoal.
plausible: Joba thinks the rich students pushed the nephew away.

meaning_en: If you are good to others, others are good to you.
conversation:
Ashraf: My new boss was strict with everyone, but after I helped her with the move, she's been kind to me every day.
Tahera: Apni bhalo to jogot bhalo.
correct: Ashraf was kind to his boss, so she has been kind to him in return.
literal: If you are fine yourself, then the whole world is also fine.
plausible: Tahera thinks the boss is only being kind to get a favour.

meaning_en: Destroying the foundation and then making superficial efforts to help.
conversation:
Tapashi: The government shut down the village schools, and now it's giving out free tablets to the children.
Shyamal: Gora kete agay jol.
correct: They destroyed the foundation and now make shallow efforts to help.
literal: Someone has cut the tree at its root and is now pouring water on its top.
plausible: Shyamal thinks the free tablets will make up for the schools.

meaning_en: The truth comes out by itself.
conversation:
Srijan: Nobody believed Tultul when she said the manager stole the funds. Yesterday his own emails were leaked.
Jayashree: Dhormer dhak batashe baje.
correct: The truth has come out on its own, just as it always does.
literal: The drum of righteousness beats by itself in the wind.
plausible: Jayashree thinks the leaked emails were faked to frame the manager.

meaning_en: The truth comes out by itself.
conversation:
Shariful: The doctor who sold fake medicines kept denying everything, and now a patient's video has gone viral.
Morsheda: Dhormer dhak batashe baje.
correct: The doctor's wrongdoing has come to light by itself in the end.
literal: The drum of dharma beats on its own when the wind blows.
plausible: Morsheda thinks the patient's viral video is staged.

meaning_en: The truth comes out by itself.
conversation:
Snehashis: Kunal claimed he wrote the hit song alone, until the real lyricist's old recordings surfaced online.
Mahi: Dhormer dhak batashe baje.
correct: The truth about the song has come out on its own in the end.
literal: The drum of righteousness begins to beat all by itself when the wind blows.
plausible: Mahi thinks the old recordings were made after the song came out.

meaning_en: A huge effort or build-up with a trivial result.
conversation:
Animikh: The company hyped its 'revolutionary' product for a year, and it turned out to be a slightly bigger phone case.
Brishti: Porboter mushik proshob.
correct: A huge build-up has ended with a disappointingly trivial result.
literal: A mountain has gone into labour and given birth to a mouse.
plausible: Brishti thinks the new phone case is a real breakthrough.

meaning_en: A huge effort or build-up with a trivial result.
conversation:
Ahsan: The ministry formed a ten-member committee and spent six months on the river report. It recommended 'further study'.
Shahida: Porboter mushik proshob.
correct: All that effort produced a ridiculously small result.
literal: After a long labour, the great mountain gave birth to a tiny mouse.
plausible: Shahida thinks further study really is the wise next step.

meaning_en: Wrongdoing always catches up with the wrongdoer.
conversation:
Debojyoti: Ten years ago Ghosh-babu cheated his brother out of the family house. Now his own son has thrown him out of it.
Sanghita: Pap bapkeo chhare na.
correct: Ghosh-babu's wrongdoing has finally caught up with him.
literal: Sin will not even spare the father of the person who committed it.
plausible: Sanghita thinks the son was unfair to throw Ghosh-babu out.

meaning_en: Planning or talking about something before it even exists.
conversation:
Mili: Didi isn't even pregnant yet, and Ma has already chosen the baby's name and school.
Sayak: Ram na jonmatei Ramayon.
correct: Ma is making big plans for something that doesn't even exist yet.
literal: The Ramayana has been written before Ram was even born.
plausible: Sayak thinks Didi has secretly told Ma she is pregnant.

meaning_en: Planning or talking about something before it even exists.
conversation:
Masum: We haven't even got the trade licence, and my partner is already designing the logo for our second branch.
Konok: Ram na jonmatei Ramayon.
correct: The partner is planning ahead for a thing that doesn't exist yet.
literal: The whole Ramayana was composed even before Ram himself had been born.
plausible: Konok thinks the second branch is a smart early plan.

proverb_bn: লেখাপড়া করে যে, গাড়িঘোড়া চড়ে সে
romanised: Lekhapora kore je, garighora chore she.
meaning_en: Education leads to success.
conversation:
Bulbul: Our neighbour's son was a rickshaw-puller's boy, and after his engineering degree he now owns two cars.
Gopa: Lekhapora kore je, garighora chore she.
correct: Getting a good education is the path to success and a better life.
literal: The boy who studied now rides in carriages and on horses.
plausible: Gopa thinks the boy became rich through luck, not learning.

proverb_bn: লেখাপড়া করে যে, গাড়িঘোড়া চড়ে সে
romanised: Lekhapora kore je, garighora chore she.
meaning_en: Education leads to success.
conversation:
Anwarul: My daughter topped her university and got a job at the World Bank. Her school friends who skipped studies are still looking for work.
Sakina: Lekhapora kore je, garighora chore she.
correct: Education has brought Anwarul's daughter real success in life.
literal: Whoever studies gets to ride in fine carriages and on horseback every day.
plausible: Sakina thinks the daughter got the job through family contacts.

proverb_bn: সাধে কি বাবা বলি, গুঁতোর চোটে বাবা বলি
romanised: Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
meaning_en: Showing respect only because one is forced to.
conversation:
Kibria: Why do you keep praising the union leader on Facebook? You hate him.
Rajon: He decides who gets the overtime. Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
correct: Rajon praises the leader only because he is forced to.
literal: He calls him father not out of love but because of the jabs.
plausible: Rajon has truly come to like the union leader after all this time.

proverb_bn: সাধে কি বাবা বলি, গুঁতোর চোটে বাবা বলি
romanised: Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
meaning_en: Showing respect only because one is forced to.
conversation:
Moyukh: The new director makes us all clap after his boring speeches, and you clap the loudest.
Faria: My appraisal is next month. Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
correct: Faria shows the director respect only because she is under pressure.
literal: She calls him father only because of the jabs, not from love.
plausible: Faria truly enjoys the director's speeches more than anyone.

proverb_bn: কেউ মরে বিল ছেঁচে, কেউ খায় কই
romanised: Keu more bil chhenche, keu khay koi.
meaning_en: One person does the hard work, another enjoys the reward.
conversation:
Sabuj: The farmers grew the rice all season, and the middlemen in the city made all the money.
Shamima: Keu more bil chhenche, keu khay koi.
correct: The farmers did the hard work while the middlemen got the reward.
literal: Someone wears himself out draining the marsh, while another eats the koi fish.
plausible: Shamima thinks the middlemen take the bigger risks in the trade.

proverb_bn: কেউ মরে বিল ছেঁচে, কেউ খায় কই
romanised: Keu more bil chhenche, keu khay koi.
meaning_en: One person does the hard work, another enjoys the reward.
conversation:
Rumpa: My sister cooked for the whole family for a week, and at the dinner everyone thanked the aunt who just set the table.
Toufiq: Keu more bil chhenche, keu khay koi.
correct: The sister did all the work, but the aunt took the credit.
literal: One person dies draining the marsh, and another eats the fish.
plausible: Toufiq thinks the aunt actually did most of the cooking for the family.

meaning_en: The very thing meant to fix a problem is itself corrupted.
conversation:
Pratim: The vigilance officer sent to catch the corrupt clerks turned out to be taking the biggest bribes himself.
Bishakha: Shorsher modhye bhut.
correct: The officer meant to stop corruption is corrupt himself.
literal: A ghost is hiding inside the mustard seeds meant to drive it out.
plausible: Bishakha thinks the clerks have framed the vigilance officer.

meaning_en: The very thing meant to fix a problem is itself corrupted.
conversation:
Kayes: The police inspector who was supposed to stop the drug trade in our area is the one running it.
Nipa: Shorsher modhye bhut.
correct: The man meant to stop the drug trade is the one behind it.
literal: The ghost is sitting right inside the mustard seeds themselves.
plausible: Nipa thinks the inspector is secretly gathering evidence against the gang.

meaning_en: Fate cannot be changed.
conversation:
Sultan: My uncle left the village to escape the floods, and the city flat he bought was flooded in its first monsoon.
Feroza: Kopaler likhon khondano jay na.
correct: The uncle could not escape the fate that was meant for him.
literal: Whatever is written on a person's forehead can never be erased by anyone.
plausible: Feroza thinks the uncle chose a badly located flat in the city.

meaning_en: Fate cannot be changed.
conversation:
Nilanjana: Mitul applied to fifty companies abroad to escape his father's shop, and he's still sitting at its counter.
Rahat: Kopaler likhon khondano jay na.
correct: Mitul hasn't been able to escape the life fate chose for him.
literal: The writing on his forehead could not be wiped off.
plausible: Rahat thinks Mitul secretly prefers working in his father's shop.

meaning_en: When you need something, you have to do things you'd rather not.
conversation:
Arkadeep: Riju hates his cousin, but he's been calling him every day since he found out the cousin works at the passport office.
Pampa: Goroj boro balai.
correct: Riju puts up with his cousin because he wants a favour.
literal: Need is a terrible plague that has come down on Riju's household.
plausible: Pampa thinks Riju and his cousin have finally made up.

meaning_en: When you need something, you have to do things you'd rather not.
conversation:
Hafiz: Rezaul swore he'd never set foot in his in-laws' house, but he's there every weekend now that his business needs his father-in-law's loan.
Dolly: Goroj boro balai.
correct: Rezaul is swallowing his pride because he wants the loan badly.
literal: Need is a dreadful curse that has fallen on Rezaul.
plausible: Dolly thinks Rezaul has truly made peace with his in-laws at last.

meaning_en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
conversation:
Masrur: When my sister moved to her husband's village, she started wearing a sari and covering her head like the women there.
Hena: Joshmin deshe jodachar.
correct: She is adapting to the local ways of the place she now lives in.
literal: Each land has its own customs, different from others.
plausible: Hena thinks the in-laws forced her to change her clothes.

meaning_en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
conversation:
Pragya: At the Bihu festival in Assam, our Kolkata group learned the dance steps and wore gamosas like everyone else.
Riyad: Joshmin deshe jodachar.
correct: The group followed the local customs of the place they visited.
literal: Every land in the world has its own particular set of customs and ways.
plausible: Riyad thinks the group was only joking around at the festival.

meaning_en: Going over the head of the proper authority.
conversation:
Mosharraf: Instead of going to the union chairman, Kalam went straight to the MP to get the road contract.
Chumki: Ghora dingiye ghas khaoa.
correct: Kalam bypassed the proper local authority and went straight to the top.
literal: Kalam leapt over the horse just to eat the grass beyond it.
plausible: Chumki thinks the union chairman had no power over the contract.

meaning_en: People's thoughts always go to what they want.
conversation:
Indraneel: We were at Didi's wedding, and Bablu kept asking when the biryani would be served.
Sreyashi: Chorer mon bonchkar dike.
correct: Bablu's mind keeps going back to the one thing he really wants.
literal: A thief's mind is always on the bundle he wants to grab.
plausible: Sreyashi thinks Bablu was hungry after travelling all day.

meaning_en: People's thoughts always go to what they want.
conversation:
Habibullah: At the funeral, my cousin kept asking who would get Dada's land.
Fatima: Chorer mon bonchkar dike.
correct: The cousin's mind is fixed on the land he wants to get for himself.
literal: A thief's thoughts are always fixed on the bundle of goods he hopes to grab.
plausible: Fatima thinks the cousin only wanted to settle things fairly.

meaning_en: An unexpected stroke of luck.
conversation:
Upasana: The lead actor fell ill on opening night, and the understudy, who had never acted on stage, got a standing ovation.
Rubab: Biraler bhagge shike chhenra.
correct: The understudy got an unexpected chance that turned into great luck.
literal: The rope holding the food basket broke, and the cat got the food.
plausible: Rubab thinks the understudy made the lead actor ill on purpose.

meaning_en: Something one is not used to feels uncomfortable.
conversation:
Karim: My mother got a new smartphone, and she's so nervous with it that she still uses the old button phone for calls.
Noor: Onobhyasher phonta kopal chorchor kore.
correct: Things you aren't used to always feel awkward and uncomfortable.
literal: A forehead not used to a tilak mark itches and burns whenever one is put on.
plausible: Noor thinks the new smartphone is badly made and keeps failing.

meaning_en: Unequal treatment for people in the same situation.
conversation:
Parijat: Both of us were late by the same ten minutes, but only I got a warning letter. Rohit got a smile.
Swagatika: Ek jatray prithok phol.
correct: Parijat was punished while Rohit, just as late, was not.
literal: Two people on the same journey ended up with different results.
plausible: Swagatika thinks Rohit had a good excuse for coming late.

meaning_en: Unequal treatment for people in the same situation.
conversation:
Pratyusha: We both scored ninety in the same exam, but the teacher praised Neel in class and ignored me.
Rafid: Ek jatray prithok phol.
correct: Pratyusha and Neel did equally well but were treated very differently.
literal: Two travellers on one trip came back with different outcomes.
plausible: Rafid thinks Neel's answers were simply written more neatly.

meaning_en: Arguing only makes a quarrel worse.
conversation:
Rokib: My wife and I fought over who forgot the gas bill, and by midnight we were shouting about our wedding day.
Moushumi: Kothay kotha bare. Stop replying.
correct: Arguing back only made the small quarrel grow into a big one.
literal: Their talking went on and on, with more and more being said.
plausible: Moushumi thinks the wedding issue needed settling anyway.

meaning_en: Arguing only makes a quarrel worse.
conversation:
Sabarna: One comment on the group chat about the football match turned into a two-day fight about politics and religion.
Rabbi: Kothay kotha bare.
correct: Each angry reply only made the online quarrel grow bigger still.
literal: The conversation in the group chat kept getting longer and longer every hour.
plausible: Rabbi thinks the group needed a serious debate on politics.

proverb_bn: পরের জন্য গর্ত খুঁড়লে নিজেকেই সে গর্তে পড়তে হয়
romanised: Porer jonno gorto khunrle nijekei she gorte porte hoy.
meaning_en: Harm planned for others comes back on you.
conversation:
Ahona: Kushal spread rumours that his colleague was stealing, and the investigation found that he was the one fiddling the accounts.
Ratul: Porer jonno gorto khunrle nijekei she gorte porte hoy.
correct: Kushal's plan to harm his colleague came back on him instead.
literal: Whoever digs a pit for someone else ends up tumbling into that pit himself.
plausible: Ratul thinks the colleague framed Kushal in the investigation.

meaning_en: Trusting the very person most likely to cause harm.
conversation:
Aftab: The cooperative made the moneylender its treasurer, the same man who charges the villagers fifty percent interest.
Reba: Sheyaler kachhe murgi borga deoa.
correct: They have trusted the person most likely to exploit the villagers.
literal: They handed over the chickens to a jackal to look after.
plausible: Reba thinks the moneylender will now lower his interest rates.

proverb_bn: সব পাখি মাছ খায়, দোষ হয় মাছরাঙার
romanised: Shob pakhi machh khay, dosh hoy machhrangar.
meaning_en: One person is blamed for what everyone does.
conversation:
Ankan: Everyone in the office takes long lunch breaks, but only Tublu got a memo for it.
Shilpa: Shob pakhi machh khay, dosh hoy machhrangar.
correct: Tublu alone is being blamed for something that everyone does.
literal: All birds eat fish, but the kingfisher is blamed.
plausible: Shilpa thinks Tublu takes far longer breaks than others.

proverb_bn: সব পাখি মাছ খায়, দোষ হয় মাছরাঙার
romanised: Shob pakhi machh khay, dosh hoy machhrangar.
meaning_en: One person is blamed for what everyone does.
conversation:
Shafiul: All the shops on our street sell without receipts, but the tax officer fined only the old tailor.
Akhi: Shob pakhi machh khay, dosh hoy machhrangar.
correct: Only the tailor is being punished for what every shop does.
literal: Every bird eats fish, yet the kingfisher is the only one that gets blamed.
plausible: Akhi thinks the tailor cheated on his taxes far more than others.

meaning_en: Passing off the same thing again and again as if it were many.
conversation:
Biswarup: The minister inaugurated the same hospital wing three times, in three different years, with three different ribbons.
Kajori: Kumirer chhana dekhano.
correct: The minister keeps passing off the same thing as something new.
literal: The minister keeps showing people the same baby crocodile.
plausible: Kajori thinks the hospital really added a new wing each of those years.

meaning_en: Using what you learned from someone against them.
conversation:
Nirjhar: Sen-babu trained Raju in the sweet-making business for ten years, and now Raju has opened a shop right next door and stolen his customers.
Gitali: Guru mara bidya.
correct: Raju is using what Sen-babu taught him to defeat Sen-babu himself.
literal: Raju learned a skill that is used for killing one's teacher.
plausible: Gitali thinks Sen-babu is happy to see Raju doing so well.

meaning_en: Using what you learned from someone against them.
conversation:
Mainul: The young lawyer who trained under Advocate Haque is now beating him in court using Haque's own arguments.
Jui: Guru mara bidya.
correct: He is defeating his old mentor with the mentor's own lessons.
literal: The young lawyer has learned a craft that kills one's own teacher.
plausible: Jui thinks Advocate Haque is losing because he has grown old.

meaning_en: Using what you learned from someone against them.
conversation:
Swarnava: I taught my nephew chess, and now he beats me every Sunday with the very openings I showed him.
Rumaisa: Guru mara bidya.
correct: The nephew is beating him with the very moves he taught.
literal: The nephew has learned a skill for killing his teacher.
plausible: Rumaisa thinks Swarnava lets his nephew win on purpose every Sunday.
